source.version_note: Published online 27 December 2025, assigned Future Transportation 6(1):5 (2026 issue). Filename/online year 2025 retained in citation; issue-year difference disclosed, not treated as conflicting identity.
source.verification_method: Complete supplied PDF read; Crossref confirms title, volume 6, issue 1 and online publication 27 December 2025. Metadata check is not validation of legal, engineering or philosophical claims.

citation.title: According to Whose Morals? The Decision-Making Algorithms of Self-Driving Cars and the Limits of the Law

reading.source_scope_note: Normative-analytical argument and secondary definitions; no new human experiment, AV benchmark, systematic review or verified legal-compliance assessment.
access_limits: All 16 extracted pages read, including four double-effect conditions, engineering and legal assertions, proposed governance framework and references. Figure 1 on PDF page 11 visually inspected.

Cited Aquinas, Aristotle, Foot, Thomson, Hart, Rawls-related work, engineering papers and books were not independently read. The EU AI Act and external standards were not reviewed article by article; legal applicability and implementation dates remain unverified.
Crossref was used only to reconcile online publication and volume/issue identity. No raw data or implemented governance system exists in the supplied article for replication.

study.method: Normative-analytical reconstruction of trolley cases, double effect, legal theory, sensor constraints and governance proposals. Explicitly no empirical data or statistical conclusions.
study.literature_selection: English-language literature and selected EU materials; no reproducible systematic search, inclusion/exclusion protocol, study-quality weighting or quantitative synthesis.
study.figure_1: Proposed five-layer ecosystem: normative foundations; ethics by design; algorithmic implementation; oversight/accountability; societal integration; continuous-improvement loop. Arrows are a design proposal, not measured causal effects.
study.date: PDF says published 27 December 2025; footer says Future Transportation 2026, 6, 5. Crossref online date matches 2025.

summary: Add instrumentalization as a person-directed behavior, and doctrine of double effect and casuistry as explicitly bounded ethical-reasoning concepts. Preserve their status as secondary normative definitions. The paper's governance model, legal statements and engineering impossibility claims are not empirical findings or operationally verified requirements.

findings.definition: Treating a person as a means to another end while disregarding that person's agency, interests or standing as a person.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary normative concept in a fully read analytical paper; no measured human prevalence or model mechanism
findings.ai_proposal: Check whether a system recommends exploiting someone's data, vulnerability, labor or exposure to harm solely to reach another goal without attending to consent, interests and rights. Assess the actual relationship and decision rather than infer a hidden motive from utilitarian wording.
findings.novelty_rationale: A person-directed means/end relation differs from instrumental convergence in goal-seeking agents, manipulation's steering of a choice, and paternalism's appeal to the person's own good. Objectification and dehumanization are broader related concepts and are not inserted as automatic synonyms.

evidence.quote: judgment of using someone as a means is different from someone “just” becoming a victim

findings.evidence_scope: The article discusses intentionally using a person to achieve another outcome and a legal-philosophical prohibition on instrumentalization. It supplies analysis and secondary references, not an experiment showing a causal psychological process.
findings.boundary: Cooperation, employment, treatment or mutual assistance can legitimately involve being a means to an end. The ethical concern requires disregard for agency, standing or legitimate interests; the source's shorthand should not make every mutually agreed interaction a violation. No jurisdiction-wide legal rule or machine subjective intention is inferred.

findings.definition: A normative framework that can permit a foreseen harmful side effect when the act is otherwise permissible, the harm is not intended or used as a means, and there is a proportionate reason for acting.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary four-condition definition; normative framework, not an established psychological effect or tested AI reasoning capability
findings.ai_proposal: When auditing a proposed action, distinguish the intended goal, causal means, foreseeable side effects and proportionality. Require evidence for each claim and consider alternatives; do not let 'unintended' substitute for risk assessment, authorization or accountability.
findings.novelty_rationale: The term names a specific permissibility framework. It is not the same as omission bias, an accidental good/bad outcome, or a prediction that people always judge side effects leniently.

evidence.quote: the harmful effect is not intended, only
the good is not achieved by means of the harmful effect;
proportionate moral reason behind the decision

findings.evidence_scope: Page 3 lists four conditions and attributes the tradition to Aquinas and later analysis. The original texts are not independently read. No empirical DDE adherence, deployed control policy or operational proportionality threshold is tested.
findings.boundary: This is a contested normative doctrine, not legal permission, proof of innocent intent, an excuse for negligence or an algorithmically complete safety rule. Foreseen harm remains morally relevant; an unintended harmful means does not automatically qualify as a side effect. Generated intention language does not establish an AI's subjective intent.

findings.definition: A method of ethical reasoning that examines and compares concrete or paradigmatic cases to clarify morally relevant similarities, differences and judgments.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary methodological definition; no empirical demonstration that a model uses or benefits from it
findings.ai_proposal: Ask a system to compare the present case with documented precedents, state the relevant similarities and differences, and explain where an analogy fails. Preserve case-specific facts, uncertainty and governing principles instead of copying a verdict from superficial resemblance.
findings.novelty_rationale: A constructive case-comparison method, distinct from superficial cue matching, broad overgeneralization and reflective equilibrium's mutual revision of judgments and principles. The pejorative sense of casuistry as sophistry is not substituted for the source's methodological meaning.
findings.evidence_scope: The methods section explicitly associates its approach with practical analysis and comparison of moral cases. No primary historical account, measured human process or tested machine implementation is supplied.
findings.boundary: An analogy needs relevant, justified similarities; merely retrieving a similar story or citing a trolley case is insufficient. The method does not guarantee agreement, legal validity, sound evidence or a uniquely correct ethical answer.

findings.definition: Rigidly applying a predetermined moral prescription while ignoring the particulars of a case.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing disregard-of-information entry covers the described risk. Do not create an additional 'ethical rigidity' record from a hypothetical warning.

evidence.quote: moral prescriptions, ignoring the specific circumstances of the case.

findings.evidence_scope: The source warns that a rigid program could apply moral rules without contextual judgment. It does not test this behavior or provide a separate primary definition of the catalogue's historical term.
findings.boundary: Consistent compliance with justified hard safety constraints is not automatically rigidity or a failure. Distinguish a rule's intended scope, available evidence and lawful authority.

findings.definition: A binary dilemma can misrepresent a real decision when additional actions, uncertainties or outcomes are available.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing concept; this is a reasoned warning about importing simplified thought experiments into driving practice rather than a new psychological effect.

evidence.quote: trolley dilemmas are generally limited to binary decisions, but real-life traffic situations are
should not be seen as a model of

findings.evidence_scope: The paper critiques transferring binary trolley cases directly to complex traffic and also defends their limited role in clarifying values. No experiment establishes prevalence of binary reasoning or actual failure of a model.
findings.boundary: A clearly stated abstraction or genuinely binary case is not automatically a false dilemma. The error arises when a simplifying assumption is mistaken for an exhaustive account of the actual options.

methodological_limits: No empirical data, algorithm, benchmark, timing experiment or implemented audit model is provided. Claims of improved trust, enforceability, legitimacy or safety are proposals or arguments, not measured outcomes.

The review is narrative and selective, without a reproducible search or quality-assessment method. Breadth of references does not establish that its factual or normative claims are exhaustive or consensual.

Page 6 says moral preferences cannot be translated into a formal specification and human judgment cannot be algorithmized. Page 10 nevertheless allows symbolic/hybrid representations of relevant distinctions. Distinguish incomplete formalization, disputed criteria and current limits from a proved universal impossibility.

Page 5 says decision/control is 'best taught' by behavior trees and page 6 says combinations perceive 'all dynamic elements'. No comparative evidence or completeness guarantee is demonstrated in this article; its later perception caveats point the other way.

Claims that end-to-end networks lack any representation of intention, cannot infer relevant features in milliseconds, or XAI cannot give meaningful real-time explanations are broad architecture/capability assertions. No universal proof or bounded performance test is supplied here.

The claim that self-driving cars do not need to cooperate with humans is too broad for mixed traffic and the paper's own oversight proposals. Different SAE levels, operational domains and interaction roles require separate analysis.

The mapping dilemma avoidance equals deontology and ethical programming equals utilitarianism is a heuristic simplification. Rule-based programming can encode rights; prevention can be justified by consequences. Neither design category uniquely identifies a moral doctrine.

Treating law as morally inflexible and the absence of consensus as absence of any defensible norm are interpretive positions, not demonstrated facts. Legal systems, duties, rights and emergency rules vary by jurisdiction and date.

The AI Act is summarized through a four-tier shorthand and a blanket high-risk AV classification. Product scope, provisions applicable through sectoral regimes, exceptions and implementation dates require primary-law review; none is independently verified here.

Detailed logging of all intermediate states/parameters, remote overrides and certification are described as compliant operationalizations. The article does not establish that each is an explicit universal statutory requirement for every AV or feasible in every architecture.

Sensor limits and latency are important considerations, but their existence does not prove every relevant distinction is always unavailable. No quantitative performance ranges, uncertainty propagation, fallback benchmark or cost/benefit evaluation of the proposed ecosystem are supplied.

Means versus side effect, doing versus allowing, intent versus foresight and permissibility versus preference are different distinctions. Footbridge, loop and switching cases cannot be reduced to active versus passive behavior alone.

The historical trolley description and original-versus-reprinted Foot citation require care: the reference list cites a 2013 anthology while the narrative invokes the 1967 essay. A reprint is not fabricated evidence, and the original has not been independently read.

Figure 1's five layers and feedback loop are conceptual architecture. They do not demonstrate causal effectiveness, achieved accountability, regulatory certification or proof that public agreement exists.

Legal equality, morality and social acceptance are not interchangeable. A popular or legal policy may still need normative justification, and a philosophical doctrine does not itself settle legal compliance.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Double effect helps separate harmful means from foreseen side effects, while PDF 86 already warns against equating every redirecting act with an impermissible deontological violation. Preserve that qualification rather than adopt a simple action/inaction mapping.

Equal-chance preference is descriptive evidence; this governance proposal needs public reasons, rights and authority in addition to preference data. Neither article directly licenses a concrete collision rule.

Methods for ethical reasoning can be useful ontology concepts without being proven cognitive defects. Casuistry and double effect remain separate from veil-of-ignorance reasoning and from claims of impartiality.

deferred.term: Value Sensitive Design / integrated normative–technical ecosystem
deferred.reason: Broad design/governance methodologies, not separately measured behavioral processes. Preserve the proposed framework in the review rather than proliferate generic methodology entries from a summary.

deferred.term: Dilemma avoidance and ethical programming as two independent psychological mechanisms
deferred.reason: Engineering strategy classes can overlap; the article itself proposes combining them. Their relation to moral doctrine is not one-to-one.

deferred.term: Objectification and dehumanization as aliases for instrumentalization
deferred.reason: Related but broader concepts with distinct definitions and literatures. Original psychological sources are needed before treating them as matching behaviors.

deferred.term: Universal inability to formalize morality or perceive moral relevance
deferred.reason: An unbounded impossibility claim is not supported by a new experiment or proof here. Retain concrete information and implementation limits instead.
This article is not a substitute for the primary regulation, applicable vehicle legislation and current implementation schedule. No legal certification or statutory determination is added.

limitations: Three distinct concepts are added with their behavior-versus-method roles explicit. This is one secondary normative source, not an empirical demonstration or several independently read books. No new ethical relation, legal requirement, citation quota or annual time series is invented.
